title: Contrapositive: why debugging is contrapositive reasoning
story:
A conditional says that if the first thing holds, the second follows. Three rearrangements of it are available and only one of them is safe.

Swapping the two halves gives the converse, which does not follow. Negating both halves in place gives the inverse, which does not follow either. Negating both halves and swapping them gives the contrapositive, and that one is not merely plausible — it is the same statement. If the second thing is absent, the first cannot have held. Anything true of the original is true of it, because they are one claim written two ways.

That is the entire logical content of debugging, and it is worth seeing why rather than being told.

Consider an invariant of the kind every system has: if this function completed correctly, then the stored balance was updated. During an incident you cannot watch the function run. What you can do is look at the stored balance, and the balance was not updated. The contrapositive converts that observation into a conclusion with no inference gap at all: the function did not complete correctly. Not probably. Not likely. The observation and the conclusion are the same fact.

Notice what makes this powerful, because it is not the certainty on its own. It is that the observation is available and the thing you wanted to know is not. You cannot inspect execution after the fact; you can inspect state. The contrapositive is the move that converts the evidence you have into a claim about the thing you cannot see, which is the position every post-hoc investigation starts from.

And the failure mode is the mirror image. Seeing the effect and concluding the suspected cause is the converse, which does not follow — the balance being wrong is consistent with that function failing and with several other things. An investigation built on the converse feels identical from the inside: a hypothesis, a symptom that matches, hours spent in a subsystem that was working the whole time. The symptom matching is not evidence, because a wrong hypothesis predicting the symptom is exactly as compatible with what you observed.

So the discipline is to phrase each step as an elimination rather than a nomination. Not 'this looks like the cause' but 'if this were working, that would be present; it is absent; so this is not working'. Each such step removes a region of the search space permanently, which is progress you keep. Nominating a suspect and looking for confirmation produces evidence that is equally consistent with being wrong, which is why it can go on for hours without converging.

One limit, because certainty at the logical level is easy to overtrust. The conclusion is only as good as the invariant. If the premise was never actually true of the system — the function can complete correctly and fail to update the balance, because another writer overwrote it, or the update is deferred, or the read was from a replica — then the deduction is valid and its conclusion is still wrong. The reasoning does not fail; the premise does. So the first question about a confident elimination is not whether the logic holds but whether the conditional it rests on was ever true.

problem.name: Reason by elimination
problem.shape: You need to know something about an execution you cannot observe, and you can observe its effects.
tell: a hypothesis was nominated because the symptom resembles it
hours have gone into a subsystem without narrowing anything
each step of the investigation adds a suspect rather than removing one
the invariant being relied on has never been stated out loud
problem.move: State the invariant as a conditional, then use the absence of its consequence to eliminate its premise. Phrase every step as 'if this were working, that would be true; it is not; so this is not working', and check the conditional itself before trusting any conclusion drawn from it.
problem.invariant: Negating both halves of a conditional and swapping them produces the same claim, so the absence of the consequence is proof of the absence of the premise. Swapping without negating, or negating without swapping, proves nothing.
problem.breaks: A valid deduction from a false premise gives a confident wrong answer. If the invariant was never true of the system — another writer overwrites the value, the update is deferred, the read came from a replica — the logic holds and the conclusion is still false, and the certainty makes it harder to revisit than a guess would have been.

cost.time: stating invariants explicitly is slower than pattern-matching on symptoms, and the useful ones are often not written down anywhere
cost.beats: nominating a likely cause and looking for confirmation, which is faster to start and produces evidence equally consistent with being wrong, and reading code from the top, which is exhaustive and does not use the observation you already have

worked.problem: Why is debugging contrapositive reasoning rather than a search for the cause?
worked.reasoning:
Because the thing you want to know is not observable and its consequences are, and the contrapositive is the only rearrangement of a conditional that lets you argue from one to the other.

Take an invariant of the kind every system has: if this function completed correctly, then the stored balance was updated. During an incident nobody can watch the function run. What is available is the stored balance, and it was not updated. Negating both halves and swapping them gives a statement identical to the original — so the function did not complete correctly, with no inference gap. The observation and the conclusion are the same fact written two ways.

What makes that valuable is not the certainty by itself. It is the direction: evidence exists about state and not about execution, and this is the move that converts the first into a claim about the second. That is the position every investigation after the fact starts from.

The failure mode is the mirror image and it is the reason this is worth naming. Seeing the effect and concluding the suspected cause swaps the halves without negating them, which proves nothing — a wrong balance is consistent with that function failing and with several other things. From the inside it feels the same: a hypothesis, a symptom that matches, hours in a subsystem that was fine. The matching is not evidence, precisely because a wrong hypothesis that predicts the symptom is equally compatible with what was observed.

So the practical form is to phrase every step as an elimination rather than a nomination. Not 'this looks like the cause' but 'if this were working, that would be present; it is absent; so this is not working'. Each such step removes a region of the search space permanently, and permanence is what makes it converge — you never have to come back. Nominating suspects and seeking confirmation can run indefinitely because nothing is ever ruled out.

The limit deserves stating, because logical certainty is easy to overtrust. The conclusion is only as good as the conditional. If the function can complete correctly and still leave the balance unchanged — another writer overwrote it, the update is deferred, the read came from a replica — then the deduction is valid and its conclusion is false. The reasoning did not fail; the premise did. Which makes the first question about any confident elimination not whether the logic holds, but whether the invariant it rests on was ever true of this system.

problem.practice: Take the last bug you chased and write down the conditional you were relying on. Then ask whether it was actually true of the system — most long debugging sessions turn out to be valid reasoning from an invariant that had an exception nobody had stated.

beats.broke: Seeing an effect and concluding the suspected cause swaps a conditional's halves without negating them, which proves nothing — so hours go into a subsystem that was working, and the matching symptom feels like evidence the whole time.
beats.fix: Use the one rearrangement that preserves the claim: if the consequence is absent, the premise did not hold. Phrase each step as an elimination, so every step removes part of the search space permanently.
beats.cost: A valid deduction from a false invariant gives a confident wrong answer, and the confidence makes it harder to revisit than a guess would have been.

interview.q: Why is debugging contrapositive reasoning rather than a search for the cause?
interview.trap: Treating a symptom that matches a hypothesis as support for it. A wrong hypothesis that predicts the same symptom is equally compatible with the observation, so matching distinguishes nothing.
interview.answer:
Because what you want to know is not observable and its consequences are, and the contrapositive is the only rearrangement of a conditional that gets you from one to the other.

Take an invariant: if this function completed correctly, the stored balance was updated. Nobody can watch the function run during an incident, but the balance is right there, and it was not updated. Negating both halves and swapping them yields a statement identical to the original, so the function did not complete correctly — no inference gap, because the observation and the conclusion are one fact written two ways.

The value is the direction rather than the certainty: evidence exists about state, the question is about execution, and this is the move that converts one into the other. That is where every investigation after the fact begins.

The failure mode is the mirror image. Seeing the effect and concluding the suspected cause swaps without negating, which proves nothing — a wrong balance is consistent with that function failing and with other things. It feels identical from inside: a hypothesis, a matching symptom, hours in a healthy subsystem. The matching is not evidence, because a wrong hypothesis predicting the symptom is equally compatible with it.

So phrase every step as an elimination rather than a nomination: if this were working, that would be present; it is absent; so this is not working. Each such step removes a region of the search space permanently, and that permanence is what makes the process converge. Nominating suspects and looking for confirmation never rules anything out, so it can run indefinitely.

The limit is worth stating because logical certainty is easy to overtrust: the conclusion is only as good as the invariant. If the function can complete correctly and still leave the balance unchanged — another writer, a deferred update, a read from a replica — the deduction is valid and the conclusion false. The premise failed, not the reasoning, which is why the first question about a confident elimination is whether the conditional it rests on was ever true.
